nice explanation.  So, we're imposing a way to parse NL by introducing spaCy.  Has it been proven that using spaCy is actually advantageous towards prediction? ie, building a model of language / the world?

really interesting question indeed.  I'm more interested if spaCy can create a "parse tree" of the NL sentence and whether this structure is useful to the logic net.  Such a tree is akin to "logical form".  It would be based on the single notion of which subtree "modifies" which node.
yes, I want to proceed, but want to know more about what you mean WM is a forest of trees, does that still retain the notion of propositions?  Can you give some examples of such tree representations?
But the tree structure may create difficulties for the design of differntiable logic rules? or how could we solve that problem?

another question is: the parse trees are found by spaCy, but when logic net produces new propositions, they either modify existing sub-trees or create lone propositions, but they cannot form new trees.  Is that a serious limitation?  What kind of differentiable mechanism allows to modify trees?
Nice!  I wonder: the generated tree is discrete -- it differs from other trees discretely.  So how could this process be differentiable?  Can you explain why this can happen?
yes, but that seems to create an exponential number of parameters as number of nodes grows... does the cost outweigh the benefits?  or is that impression not correct?

/us                so, do we have a comprehensive list of NL templates? They seem to come from Chomskyan linguistics.  What happens if our model encounters informal grammatical patterns not fitting the templates?

After some more research, it seems that we want WM to have more "links" in the form of trees or graphs, but such links can be realized by the use of indexed entities.  Our first-order logic rules or rewrite rules still can do the job, but it must do "soft" matching over the entire WM.  The computation scales as O(N²) with N being WM size in nodes, though the # parameters can be much smaller. After some more research, it seems that we want WM to have more "links" in the form of trees or graphs, but such links can be realized by the use of indexed entities.  Our first-order logic rules or rewrite rules still can do the job, but it must do "soft" matching over the entire WM.  The computation scales as O(N²) with N being WM size in nodes, though the # parameters can be much smaller. I don't have a conclusion yet but that takes us closer.  Secondly, the parsing of NL to and from our internal representation are symmetric in the "inverse function" sense, is it possible to exploit this, eg. by using reversible logic rules, or just doing the training symmetrically?

Good analysis. Particularly intriguing is the symmetric NL parsing assumption.  What do you mean by "cycle"?  That assumption must be wrong because there are often many ways to express a meaning. I'm still thinking... if we are doing AR training, we are forcing the generated text to be identical to the input text, right?  But could we modify the objective of AR to accomodate for the one-to-many nature of NL generation?
